_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning to develop questions that help us investigate issues about economics, business, work, or money.

Convergent strip of extended-junk suffixes from 10 MC answer field(s).

toLevel2.question: A targeted research question has no advantage over a vague one when investigating an economic issue.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Targeted questions guide investigation toward useful evidence and clearer answers than vague ones.

distractors.explanation: Treating targeted questions as no better than vague ones ignores how focus shapes investigation.

toLevel2.question: Asking 'Who benefits?' has no link to investigating any issue about money or work in any setting.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Who benefits?' is a core question that shapes economic investigation by revealing winners.

distractors.explanation: Treating 'Who benefits?' as unrelated ignores how it focuses an investigation.

toLevel2.question: A research question can ask why one product costs more than another similar product.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing prices across products is a strong starting question for an economic investigation.

distractors.explanation: This is a recognised type of investigation question at this level.

toLevel2.question: Investigation begins with curiosity, and good questions often lead to meaningful answers.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Curiosity drives investigation, and well-formed questions point to evidence and answers.

distractors.explanation: This is the standard description of how investigation begins in economic study.

toLevel2.question: Forming a question about a news story has no use at all when planning a class investigation.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: News stories provide real, current issues that students can shape into investigation questions.

distractors.explanation: Treating news stories as useless misses a rich source of investigation questions.

toLevel2.question: Asking 'Who is disadvantaged?' helps a student see who loses out in an economic issue.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Who is disadvantaged?' reveals who loses out in an issue and balances 'Who benefits?'

distractors.explanation: This question is a recognised tool for spotting harm in an economic situation.

toLevel2.question: Every question about an economic issue is exactly the same and gives the same answer in every case.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Different questions lead to different evidence and different answers; questions vary widely.

distractors.explanation: Treating all questions as identical ignores how question wording shapes investigation.

toLevel2.question: A question about how work in a local area has changed over time can guide a class investigation.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Local change-over-time questions are strong starting points for an economic investigation.

distractors.explanation: This is one of the recognised question types at this level.

toLevel2.question: A question that asks 'why do prices differ?' has no connection to investigating any economic issue.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Why do prices differ?' is a strong investigation question that guides comparison and evidence.

distractors.explanation: Treating this question as unconnected ignores how it shapes price-focused investigation.

toLevel2.question: Curiosity, careful wording, and a clear focus all support the development of a useful research question.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Curiosity, careful wording, and a clear focus together produce useful research questions.

distractors.explanation: These three features are widely taught as the basis of strong question development.

toLevel2.question: Asking 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' always means giving exactly the same answer for both.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' look at different sides of an issue and yield different answers.

distractors.explanation: Treating the two questions as identical misses how each one looks at a different side.

toLevel2.question: A question about where school funding comes from and how it is spent has no link to any real investigation.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: School funding questions support real investigation by directing attention to income and spending.

distractors.explanation: Treating funding questions as unrelated to real investigation ignores their direct value as practice.

toLevel2.question: What is the role of a research question in an economic investigation?
toLevel2.correct: A research question guides what evidence the investigator looks for and what answer is sought
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A research question guides what evidence is collected and what answer is sought.

distractors.answer: A research question has no link to any evidence the investigator gathers in any way at any time
distractors.explanation: A research question is directly linked to the evidence used; the link is fundamental.

distractors.answer: A research question always gives the answer at the start so no investigation is ever needed
distractors.explanation: A research question prompts an investigation; it does not give the answer at the start.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is a strong example of an economic research question?
toLevel2.correct: Why does one brand of trainers cost more than a similar brand sold in the same shop?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing two brands of trainers in the same shop is a strong, targeted research question.

distractors.answer: Why are things in the world the way that things are in the world for many different reasons?
distractors.explanation: This question is too vague and does not focus on any clear economic issue.

distractors.answer: Why is it that everything always works in some way for someone somewhere at any time?
distractors.explanation: This question is too broad to guide an investigation at this level.

toLevel2.question: Which question best helps a student see who loses out in an economic issue?
toLevel2.correct: Who is disadvantaged by this decision in the local community at this point in time?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Who is disadvantaged?' directly reveals who loses out in an economic issue.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the wall in the local council building during the year of the decision?
distractors.explanation: Wall colour has no link to who loses out in an economic issue.

distractors.answer: How many cars pass the school gate during the morning bell on a single Tuesday in spring?
distractors.explanation: Counting cars has no link to who loses out in an economic issue.

toLevel2.question: Which question best helps a student see who gains in an economic issue?
toLevel2.correct: Who benefits most from this decision in the local community at this point in time?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: 'Who benefits?' directly reveals who gains in an economic issue.

distractors.answer: Which book on the shelf was read first by the youngest student in the class on Monday?
distractors.explanation: Books on a shelf have no link to who gains in an economic issue.

distractors.answer: What is the height of the trees in the park behind the school during the autumn months?
distractors.explanation: Tree heights have no link to who gains in an economic issue.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes a vague research question?
toLevel2.correct: A question that does not focus on a single clear issue and so produces unclear evidence and answers
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A vague question does not focus on a single issue and produces unclear evidence and answers.

distractors.answer: A question that focuses on one clear issue and produces evidence and answers easily for the class
distractors.explanation: Focused questions are clear, not vague; this option describes the opposite.

distractors.answer: A question that always gives the same answer as every other question that any student ever asks
distractors.explanation: Different questions yield different answers; this generalisation is wrong.

toLevel2.question: Why might a question about a news story support a class investigation?
toLevel2.correct: News stories give real, current issues that students can shape into clear investigation questions
toLevel2.correctExplanation: News stories give real, current issues that students can shape into investigation questions.

distractors.answer: News stories have no link to any real issue and so they never support any investigation
distractors.explanation: News stories report real issues; they directly support investigation.

distractors.answer: News stories always give the answer at the start so no investigation is ever needed at any time
distractors.explanation: News stories raise issues but do not give every answer; investigation is still needed.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best example of a clear focus in a research question?
toLevel2.correct: A single issue, a single time, and a single place named clearly in the wording of the question
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A single issue, a single time, and a single place is a clear focus for a research question.

distractors.answer: Many issues, many times, and many places listed at once in the wording of the question
distractors.explanation: Many issues, times, and places at once make a question harder to investigate.

distractors.answer: No issue, no time, and no place named in the wording of the question
distractors.explanation: Without an issue, time, or place, the question is too vague to investigate.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is a research question about work in a local area?
toLevel2.correct: How has paid work in our local area changed over the last fifty years for the older generation?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Asking how paid work has changed over fifty years for an older generation is a strong question.

distractors.answer: How many clouds pass over the local area on a single afternoon in autumn each year for ten years?
distractors.explanation: Counting clouds has no link to investigating work in a local area.

distractors.answer: What is the name of every bird that has ever flown over the local area in any direction?
distractors.explanation: Naming every bird ever has no link to investigating work in a local area.

toLevel2.question: Which question best supports an investigation about school funding?
toLevel2.correct: Where does the funding for our school come from and how is the money spent each year?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Asking where funding comes from and how it is spent supports a school funding investigation.

distractors.answer: What colour is the front gate of every school in every town in every state at any time?
distractors.explanation: Gate colour has no link to investigating school funding.

distractors.answer: How tall is each tree on the school grounds during the autumn months of each year for ten years?
distractors.explanation: Tree heights have no link to investigating school funding.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following is the best starting point for an economic investigation?
toLevel2.correct: A clear, targeted question that names the issue, the place, and the time the investigator wants to study
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A clear, targeted question naming issue, place, and time is the best starting point.

distractors.answer: A vague wish to learn something about everything in the world without any clear focus on any issue
distractors.explanation: A vague wish without focus is hard to turn into a workable investigation.

distractors.answer: A demand that someone else find every answer before any question is even formed at any time
distractors.explanation: Demanding answers before forming questions is the opposite of investigation.

toLevel2.question: Which one of the following best describes the role of curiosity in an investigation?
toLevel2.correct: Curiosity drives an investigator to ask questions, look for evidence, and seek meaningful answers
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Curiosity drives an investigator to ask questions, look for evidence, and seek answers.

distractors.answer: Curiosity has no link to asking questions, finding evidence, or seeking any answer at any time
distractors.explanation: Curiosity is directly linked to asking questions and finding evidence.

distractors.answer: Curiosity always blocks an investigation by stopping every student from asking any question
distractors.explanation: Curiosity supports rather than blocks question-asking in an investigation.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only useful question types for an economic investigation?
toLevel2.correct: Why-questions, who-benefits questions, who-is-disadvantaged questions, and how-has-it-changed questions
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Why, who-benefits, who-is-disadvantaged, and how-has-it-changed are useful investigation question types.

distractors.answer: Cloud-counting questions, bird-naming questions, and gate-colour questions across every town and time
distractors.explanation: These questions have no link to any economic issue or to any investigation.

distractors.answer: No-question-at-all approaches, demands for answers without questions, and refusals to investigate
distractors.explanation: These approaches are the opposite of investigation; they avoid asking questions.

toLevel2.sentence: A research {{blank:1}} guides what evidence the investigator looks for and a clear {{blank:2}} keeps the investigation on one issue.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not a guiding sentence in an investigation.
Fixture is a scheduled match, not a guiding sentence in an investigation.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not the centre of an investigation.
Fixture is a scheduled match, not the centre of an investigation.

toLevel2.sentence: Asking 'Who {{blank:1}}?' shows who gains in an issue, and asking 'Who is {{blank:2}}?' shows who loses out.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniforms are clothing, not the act of gaining from an issue.
Scores are points in a match, not the act of gaining from an issue.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.explanation: Uniformed describes clothing, not the state of losing out.
Scored describes a competition outcome, not the state of losing out.

toLevel3.question: A student asking 'Why does one product cost more than another?' is forming a question that supports comparison.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparison questions support investigation by directing attention to clear differences between products.

distractors.explanation: Comparison questions are recognised as strong starting points for economic investigation.

toLevel3.question: Asking 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' always reveals exactly the same group of people in any case.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: These two questions look at different sides of an issue and almost always reveal different groups.

distractors.explanation: Treating both questions as identical ignores how each one targets a different side of the issue.

toLevel3.question: A question about a financial news story can be used to plan a clear class investigation each week.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: News stories provide real, current issues that translate well into class investigation questions.

distractors.explanation: News-based questions are widely used as a starting point for economic investigation.

toLevel3.question: Vague research questions always lead to clearer answers than targeted, well-worded research questions in every case.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Targeted questions usually lead to clearer answers than vague ones; vague questions blur evidence.

distractors.explanation: Treating vague questions as clearer ignores how careful wording focuses investigation.

toLevel3.question: A question about how local work has changed over time has no link to interviewing community members in any way.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Change-over-time questions support investigation through interviews, archives, and local records.

distractors.explanation: Treating these questions as unrelated to interviews ignores how they connect investigation to local sources.

toLevel3.question: Asking 'Why does this business succeed while another does not?' has no link to any economic investigation in any setting.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Success-vs-failure questions are widely used in economic investigation to compare two cases.

distractors.explanation: Treating success-vs-failure questions as unrelated misses a recognised investigation approach.

toLevel3.question: A question that targets one clear issue is usually easier to investigate than a question that mixes several issues at once.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Single-issue questions focus evidence collection; mixed questions scatter attention across many issues.

distractors.explanation: Single-focus questions are widely taught as easier to investigate than mixed-focus ones.

toLevel3.question: Forming a research question about school funding has no link to any real-world investigation skill at all in any setting.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: School funding questions are real, useful investigation questions that build skill at this level.

distractors.explanation: Treating funding questions as unconnected ignores their direct value as investigation practice.

toLevel3.question: Mia wants to investigate why one snack costs more than another at the canteen. Which research question best fits her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What features of the two snacks at the canteen could explain the price difference between them?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about features that could explain a price difference is a strong, targeted investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the wall behind the canteen on every Friday afternoon for the whole year?
distractors.explanation: Wall colour has no link to a price difference between two snacks at the canteen.

distractors.answer: How many birds visit the school garden during the lunch break on a single day in spring each year?
distractors.explanation: Counting birds has no link to a price difference between two snacks at the canteen.

toLevel3.question: Jarrah wants to know who benefits and who loses out from a new local market plan. Which pair of questions fits his investigation?
toLevel3.correct: Who benefits from this market plan, and who is disadvantaged by it in the local community?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' is the right pair for this investigation.

distractors.answer: Who reads the longest book in the school library, and who runs the fastest in the playground each week?
distractors.explanation: Library and playground questions have no link to a local market plan.

distractors.answer: Who picked the brightest jacket on a Tuesday morning, and who walked the slowest through the school gates?
distractors.explanation: Jacket and gate questions have no link to a local market plan.

toLevel3.question: Anika wants to investigate how paid work has changed in her area over fifty years. Which question best fits her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What kinds of paid work have appeared and disappeared in our area over the last fifty years for adults?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking what paid work has appeared and disappeared over fifty years is a strong investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the brightest colour on every house roof in every town across every state of the country?
distractors.explanation: House roof colours have no link to changes in paid work over time in a local area.

distractors.answer: How long does the wind blow each afternoon during the autumn months of each year for ten years?
distractors.explanation: Wind length has no link to changes in paid work over time in a local area.

toLevel3.question: Sam reads a news story about a local business closing. Which research question best supports a class investigation?
toLevel3.correct: What economic factors led the local business to close, and who is affected by that closure?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about the economic factors and who is affected fits a strong investigation of a closure.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the front door of the local business on a single Friday afternoon in autumn?
distractors.explanation: Door colour has no link to economic factors behind a business closing.

distractors.answer: How many clouds pass over the local business each morning during the spring months of one year?
distractors.explanation: Counting clouds has no link to economic factors behind a business closing.

toLevel3.question: Lila wants to compare two businesses in her area, one that is doing well and one that is struggling. Which research question best fits her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What are the main differences in how each business operates that could explain their different results?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about differences in operations is a strong, targeted comparison question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the front sign on each business at the end of last week?
distractors.explanation: Sign colour has no link to differences in business operations or results.

distractors.answer: How many birds visit each business roof during the autumn months over a stretch of ten whole years?
distractors.explanation: Birds on roofs have no link to differences in business operations or results.

toLevel3.question: Kofi wants to investigate where school funding comes from and how it is used. Which research question best fits his plan?
toLevel3.correct: Where does the funding for our school come from each year, and how is the money spent?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking where funding comes from and how it is decided is a strong investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of every chair in every classroom in every school across the whole country in any year?
distractors.explanation: Chair colour has no link to school funding sources or to how funding is decided.

distractors.answer: How fast does the wind blow across the school yard each afternoon during the autumn months for ten years?
distractors.explanation: Wind speed has no link to school funding sources or to how funding is decided.

toLevel3.question: Yen reads a news story about young people and saving. Which question best supports a useful investigation?
toLevel3.correct: What habits help young people in our area save money, and what challenges make saving difficult for them?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about saving habits and challenges among young people is a strong investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the front fence at every house in every town in every state in the country?
distractors.explanation: Fence colour has no link to young people's saving habits or challenges.

distractors.answer: How long does each cloud last in the sky above our area during the autumn months for one full year?
distractors.explanation: Cloud length has no link to young people's saving habits or challenges.

toLevel3.question: Rosa wants to investigate why some shops have lower prices than others. Which research question best supports her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What economic factors lead some shops to charge lower prices than other shops for similar items?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about economic factors behind lower prices is a strong, targeted investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the brightest paint colour on each shop's front wall during the autumn months across one year?
distractors.explanation: Paint colour has no link to why some shops charge lower prices than others.

distractors.answer: How many leaves fall outside each shop during the autumn months across one full year in our local area?
distractors.explanation: Falling leaves have no link to why some shops charge lower prices than others.

toLevel3.question: Amir wants to investigate how one new business is changing the local area. Which research question fits his plan best?
toLevel3.correct: How has the new business affected jobs, prices, and choices for shoppers in our local area so far?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about effects on jobs, prices, and choices is a strong investigation question for a new business.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of the new business front sign on a single Friday morning during the autumn season?
distractors.explanation: Sign colour has no link to a business's economic effects on a local area.

distractors.answer: How many birds visit the new business roof during the spring months of one full year in our local area?
distractors.explanation: Birds on a roof have no link to a business's economic effects on a local area.

toLevel3.question: Jade wants to investigate why one product became popular while a similar product did not. Which research question fits her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What features, prices, and advertising helped one product become popular while a similar product did not?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about features, prices, and advertising that drove one product's popularity is a strong question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of every wrapper of every product at every shop on a Tuesday morning each spring?
distractors.explanation: Wrapper colour has no link to why one product became popular over another.

distractors.answer: How many leaves fell next to every product at every shop during the autumn months in any one year?
distractors.explanation: Falling leaves have no link to why one product became popular over another.

toLevel3.question: Linh wants to compare paid work in two different local areas. Which research question best fits her plan?
toLevel3.correct: What kinds of paid work are most common in each area, and how do the two patterns of work differ?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking about common paid work in each area and how the patterns differ is a strong comparison question.

distractors.answer: What is the brightest colour of paint on every wall in every town in every state of the country?
distractors.explanation: Paint colour has no link to paid work patterns in any local area.

distractors.answer: How many clouds pass over each area during the autumn months across a stretch of ten whole years?
distractors.explanation: Counting clouds has no link to paid work patterns in any local area.

toLevel3.question: Marcus wants to investigate a financial issue in the news. Which research question best supports a class investigation?
toLevel3.correct: What is the financial issue, who is affected by it, and what choices does the community now face?
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Asking what the issue is, who is affected, and what choices follow is a strong investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of every newspaper page on every day in every town in every state of the country?
distractors.explanation: Newspaper page colour has no link to a financial issue in the news.

distractors.answer: How many leaves fall outside every newsstand each autumn for ten whole years across our local area?
distractors.explanation: Falling leaves have no link to a financial issue in the news.

toLevel4.question: Anika investigates why a brand of trainers costs more by forming a clear question and listing sources of evidence to check.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Forming a clear question and listing sources is a strong example of investigation in action.

distractors.explanation: Anika is using two core investigation skills: question forming and source planning.

toLevel4.question: Sam asks the question 'Why are things?' and then plans a clear class investigation around that single broad question alone.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: 'Why are things?' is too vague to support a clear investigation; targeted wording is needed.

distractors.explanation: Treating a vague question as enough ignores the role of targeted wording in investigation.

toLevel4.question: Anika wants to investigate why a brand of trainers costs more. She forms a clear question and lists sources of evidence to check. Which idea best fits her work?
toLevel4.correct: She is using two core investigation skills: targeted question forming and source planning
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Forming a clear question and listing sources are two core investigation skills.

distractors.answer: She is using a single one-off action that has no link to any investigation skill at any time
distractors.explanation: Combining a question with a source plan is a method, not a one-off action.

distractors.answer: She is using a school rule that bans every student from asking any question at any time
distractors.explanation: There is no such school rule; she is using planned investigation skills by choice.

toLevel4.question: Sam asks 'Why are things?' and plans a class investigation around that single broad question. Which response best evaluates his plan?
toLevel4.correct: The question is too vague to guide a class investigation; clearer wording focused on one issue is needed
toLevel4.correctExplanation: 'Why are things?' is too vague; investigation needs targeted wording focused on one clear issue.

distractors.answer: The question is fully clear and focuses the class investigation directly on a single economic issue at once
distractors.explanation: The question is vague rather than focused; it does not name an issue clearly.

distractors.answer: The question is the strongest possible starting point because no further wording can ever improve any question
distractors.explanation: Question wording can almost always be improved to better focus an investigation.

toLevel4.question: Lila reads a news story about young people and saving and wants to plan an investigation. Which strategy best supports her plan?
toLevel4.correct: Form a targeted question about saving habits and challenges for young people in her local area
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Forming a targeted question about local saving habits and challenges supports a clear investigation.

distractors.answer: Form no question and demand that someone else find all the answers without any planning
distractors.explanation: Demanding answers without forming questions is the opposite of investigation.

distractors.answer: Form a single broad question with no focus on any issue, place, or time in any setting
distractors.explanation: Broad, unfocused questions are hard to turn into workable class investigations.

toLevel4.question: Kofi wants to compare two snacks at the canteen by price. Which research question best supports a class investigation?
toLevel4.correct: What features of each snack at the canteen could explain the price difference between them?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Asking about features that could explain a price difference is a strong, targeted investigation question.

distractors.answer: What is the colour of every snack wrapper at every canteen across every state of the country?
distractors.explanation: Wrapper colour has no link to a snack price difference at the canteen.

distractors.answer: How many leaves fell outside the canteen during the autumn months over a stretch of ten whole years?
distractors.explanation: Falling leaves have no link to a snack price difference at the canteen.

toLevel4.question: Yen wants to know who gains and who loses out from a new local market plan. Which research approach best fits her plan?
toLevel4.correct: Use 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' as paired questions to map both sides of the issue
toLevel4.correctExplanation: 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' are paired questions that map both sides of an issue.

distractors.answer: Use a single question with no focus on any side of the issue or on any community group
distractors.explanation: An unfocused question fails to map the sides of the issue at all.

distractors.answer: Use no question and ignore the issue completely so no investigation is ever started or planned
distractors.explanation: Ignoring the issue is the opposite of starting an investigation.

toLevel4.question: Rosa wants to investigate how paid work in her area has changed over fifty years. Which strategy best fits her plan?
toLevel4.correct: Form a targeted change-over-time question and plan to interview older community members for evidence
toLevel4.correctExplanation: A targeted change-over-time question with planned interviews is a strong investigation strategy.

distractors.answer: Form a vague question with no focus on time or place and skip every interview with any community member
distractors.explanation: Vague questions and skipping interviews weaken rather than support investigation.

distractors.explanation: Refusing to ask questions or talk to community members is the opposite of investigation.

toLevel4.question: Amir is told that 'Who benefits?' and 'Who is disadvantaged?' always reveal exactly the same group. Which response best evaluates this claim?

distractors.answer: The claim is correct because the two questions always point to exactly the same group in every economic case

toLevel4.question: Linh wants to investigate where her school funding comes from. Which strategy best supports a clear investigation?
